title: A cloud holds about 500 tonnes of water. Why doesn't it fall? | So That's Why
description:
At 2 p.m. on a summer afternoon the sun is blazing; by 3 p.m. it's pouring. That cloud you see when you look up really does hold water: an ordinary cumulus cloud has an estimated 500 tonnes or so. Water is heavier than air, so how does it stay up in the sky? And how does it turn into the heavy rain hitting you in under an hour?

In this episode, the Chief and Little Q start from a single drop of water in a cloud: how water vapour differs from a cloud, why a cloud droplet falls only about 1 cm a second, why one raindrop takes about a million cloud droplets, why thunderstorms come in the afternoon, and why they often stop so soon. At the end, three things to watch for when you look up.

The illustrations in this episode were made with AI. The numbers are estimates for typical cases, and real clouds vary a lot; the source of every number is listed in the references below.

p001.text: Chief! Chief! The cloud by my balcony keeps growing up!

p002.text: It was all white, and now its bottom's turned grey.

p003.text: Better bring the laundry in soon.

p004.text: But I don't get it. Is there really water in a cloud?

p005.text: Yes, lots. An ordinary cumulus cloud holds about 500 tonnes of water.

p006.text: You've seen the answer every summer. Nobody told you, that's all.

p007.text: First, a guess: 500 tonnes is how many elephants?

p008.text: And will it fall on you as rain? How soon?

p010.text: So why doesn't the whole thing fall down?

p011.text: This morning, that cloud didn't exist. The sky was clear, not one cloud.

p012.text: The sun heats the ground; the ground heats the air above it.

p013.text: So where do clouds come from? Is it water vapour?

p014.text: Many people think so. But look at this.

p015.text: When a kettle boils, the bit right by the spout is see-through.

p016.text: The white mist only shows up a little way out.

p017.text: So the white stuff isn't water vapour?

p018.text: Right. Real water vapour is invisible. The white is vapour cooled back into tiny drops.

p019.text: Clouds are the same: lots of tiny drops, sometimes tiny ice crystals, not a gas.

p020.text: But there's no kettle in the sky. What cools it down?

p021.text: It climbs. Sun-warmed air is lighter than the air around it, so it rises in bubbles.

p023.text: Sort of. And you've felt it: the higher you climb a mountain, the cooler it gets.

p024.text: Rising air meets lower pressure, so it expands; and expanding cools it.

p025.text: Before it condenses, rising air cools about 10 °C for every kilometre it climbs.

p026.text: At some height the air is saturated; the extra vapour condenses.

p027.text: Like the drops on a cold drink's cup in summer.

p028.text: Drops stick to the cup. What do they stick to up there?

p029.text: Good question. Air is full of specks you can't see: dust, sea salt, smoke.

p030.text: The vapour condenses on those specks into tiny drops.

p031.text: So cumulus clouds often have flat bases: that height is where air gets cold enough to condense.

p032.text: It's true! They all have the same flat bottoms!

p033.text: While warm air keeps coming up from below, the cloud keeps growing, like a cauliflower.

p035.text: Let's work it out for an ordinary cumulus cloud. Say it's a big box, one kilometre long, wide and high.

p036.text: The water in a cloud is thin: about half a gram per cubic metre.

p037.text: But a cubic kilometre is a billion cubic metres.

p038.text: A billion times half a gram... how much is that?

p040.text: About as heavy as a hundred elephants.

p042.text: Sounds scary, right? One might be over your house right now.

p044.text: Yes, even more. That same cubic kilometre of air weighs about a million tonnes.

p045.text: So the water is just a tiny bit mixed into the air?

p046.text: Right. And the water isn't one big lump. It's split into tons of bits.

p047.text: A typical cloud droplet is about two hundredths of a millimetre across, several times thinner than a hair.

p048.text: So it's so small it doesn't weigh anything?

p049.text: It does have weight, and it really is falling. Just very, very slowly.

p050.text: Think: drop a stone and a feather together. Which lands first?

p052.text: Smaller things, the more air resists.

p053.text: Droplet-sized, the air almost holds it up.

p054.text: In still air, a cloud droplet falls only about 1 cm per second.

p056.text: At that speed, falling from a cloud base 1 km up would take over a day.

p057.text: And it dries up on the way before it lands.

p058.text: But the cloud stays all afternoon. It doesn't slowly sink.

p059.text: Because the air in that cloud isn't still. Remember the warm air that keeps rising?

p060.text: In a growing cumulus cloud, the rising air can move several metres a second.

p061.text: So it's riding an elevator up!

p062.text: Exactly. A cloud has weight, but its water is in countless bits, each light enough for air to hold.

p063.text: How big must a drop get to be too heavy?

p064.text: Raindrops you've felt are often about 2 mm: 100 times a droplet's width.

p066.text: That's the width. For volume, you multiply in all three directions.

p067.text: A hundred times a hundred, times a hundred, is a million.

p070.text: How do they get together? Does someone squish them?

p071.text: Nobody squishes them. They bump together.

p072.text: Cloud drops come in many sizes. Big ones fall faster, so they catch and hit smaller ones below.

p073.text: They stick, it gets bigger, falls faster, hits more.

p075.text: Just like that. It's called collision and coalescence. But that's only one way.

p076.text: High enough up, a cloud gets below 0 °C. There are tiny ice crystals,

p077.text: and drops colder than 0 °C that still aren't frozen.

p079.text: Yes, that's common in clouds. And there, ice crystals grab vapour better than drops do.

p080.text: The crystals grow as they fall, then melt into rain in the warmer air lower down.

p081.text: So my rain might have been snow?

p082.text: It might. In tall summer storm clouds, both ways can happen.

p083.text: Either way, the drops must grow big enough first.

p084.text: Once they're big, does the whole cloud fall?

p085.text: When a cloud rains, it's still there, right?

p087.text: What falls is the big drops.

p088.text: Too heavy for the rising air, they fall out the cloud base.

p089.text: Raindrops fall 6 to 7 m a second, hundreds of times faster than droplets.

p090.text: The cloud stays put. Only the grown drops leave, batch by batch.

p091.text: But near my house, some clouds rain, some never do.

p093.text: Back to the start: how tall the cloud grows, and how hard the air inside rushes up.

p094.text: The small, flat white clouds of fine days can't grow tall, so they fade before their drops grow.

p095.text: Heavy rain comes from tall clouds.

p096.text: Their tops pass 10 km, as high as airliners or higher.

p097.text: That high! That needs lots of warm air.

p098.text: Yes. So guess: when is the ground hottest in a day?

p100.text: Lots of people guess that. The sun is highest at noon, but the ground and air get hottest later.

p101.text: Like a pan on the stove: it isn't hottest right away. It takes a while.

p102.text: So warm air rises hardest in the afternoon.

p104.text: Taiwan's summer has two more helpers: damp air blowing in from the sea,

p105.text: and mountains. Slopes push air up, so clouds grow easily by mountains.

p106.text: So at three in the afternoon, that cloud outside my house... turned grey!

p107.text: Yes. It's so tall and thick that sunlight can't pass, so its base looks grey.

p108.text: Why do storms often stop so fast?

p109.text: Because a big rain turns off its engine.

p110.text: Falling rain drags the air around it down; rain drying up on the way makes that air even colder.

p111.text: The cool wind before a storm is often this air hitting the ground.

p112.text: I know that wind! Then it rains!

p113.text: Cold air pours down and blocks the warm air.

p114.text: No warm air, so the cloud runs down.

p116.text: A single storm cloud often grows and fades away in under an hour.

p117.text: But it's not like this every afternoon.

p118.text: How damp the air is, how cold it is up high, how the wind blows: if one is wrong, the cloud can't grow.

p119.text: So how do I know if today's clouds will rain?

p120.text: Chief! Its top is still bubbling up!

p121.text: The cauliflower? It means air's still rising.

p122.text: Just look up to see it.

p123.text: Now the top's gone flat and it's spreading out!

p124.text: Like an anvil. It's grown up to a layer it can hardly get past.

p125.text: Whoa, it's suddenly so cool! The laundry's flying!

p126.text: Remember that cool wind? Cold air outruns the rain. What did I say?

p128.text: Big drops! Are raindrops pointy, like tears?

p130.text: The faster a drop falls, the harder air pushes up.

p131.text: Small ones are nearly round. Bigger ones get flat bottoms, like a hamburger bun.

p132.text: Any bigger and they're torn into pieces. So raindrops can't grow forever.

p133.text: So what hit my hand was a hamburger bun!

p134.text: Laundry's in, and the rain stopped. Under an hour!

p137.text: Every drop that hit your hand was about a million droplets put together.

p138.text: Remember the tiny drops? They do fall. They wait to grow!

p140.text: When do storms start near you? Tell us below.
